clinicalScope: Vaccination practice and management in low‑resource East African hospitals
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Vaccines are biological preparations that train the immune system to fight specific infections. In low‑resource East Africa, they are the first line of defence against common childhood and adult diseases, but challenges like cold‑chain failure, limited laboratory support and vaccine hesitancy affect coverage.

sections.p: Vaccines are grouped by the type of antigen and the method of preparation.
b: Live attenuated – e.g. MMR, BCG; induce strong cellular and humoral immunity
Inactivated – e.g. inactivated influenza, polio; safe in immunocompromised
Toxoid – e.g. tetanus, diphtheria; neutralise bacterial toxins
Subunit/ conjugate – e.g. Hib, PCV; use purified protein with carrier

sections.p: Vaccines contain antigens that mimic the pathogen’s key surface molecules.
b: Live vaccines contain whole weakened organisms; may replicate locally
Inactivated vaccines contain killed whole virus or bacterial fragments
Toxoids are chemically modified toxins that retain antigenicity but lose toxicity
Subunit vaccines use purified proteins or polysaccharides linked to carrier proteins

t.b: Higher load may improve seroconversion but increase reactogenicity

sections.p: The protective antigens are selected for their ability to elicit neutralising antibodies and memory T cells.
b: Surface proteins (e.g. hemagglutinin, neuraminidase in influenza)

t.b: Enhances immune response, allows dose sparing

sections.p: Vaccines target pathogens that spread via droplets, contact or vectors common in East Africa.
b: Polio – fecal‑oral; endemic in some rural areas
Typhoid – contaminated water; high prevalence in informal settlements
COVID‑19 – respiratory droplets; vaccine rollout delayed

t.b: Loss of potency; leads to sub‑optimal immunity

sections.p: Vaccination mimics natural infection, priming B and T cells without causing disease.
b: Antigen presentation by dendritic cells activates naïve T cells
B cells produce specific IgG and IgM; memory B cells persist
Cell‑mediated immunity (CD4+, CD8+) crucial for viral and intracellular bacteria

sections.p: Vaccines are generally safe; adverse events are rare and usually mild.
Serological testing confirms vaccine response when needed.
No specific treatment for vaccine reactions; manage symptomatically.
Vaccine failure can be due to pathogen evolution or host factors.
b: Antigenic drift in influenza reduces match

sections.p: Immunisation programmes reduce morbidity and mortality; require community engagement.
b: Routine childhood schedule (BCG, OPV, DTP, Hib, PCV, MMR, IPV)

sections.p: Rare but serious complications can occur.
Assess knowledge of schedules, contraindications, and emergency management.
b: Recall WHO schedule for a child with missed doses
Explain cold‑chain steps and consequences of failure

whenToSeekHelp: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), high fever >39°C with rash, persistent vomiting after vaccination

faq.q: Why is the influenza vaccine reformulated each year?
faq.a: Because influenza viruses mutate rapidly; annual updates match circulating strains.

faq.q: Can I give a live vaccine to a patient with HIV?
faq.a: No, live vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised patients.

faq.q: What should I do if the cold‑chain is broken?
faq.a: Assess vaccine potency if possible; consider revaccination and reinforce storage protocols.

exam: What is the WHO target coverage for routine childhood immunisation? — 90% to achieve herd immunity
Which vaccine is contraindicated in a 5‑year‑old with severe eczema? — Live attenuated (e.g., MMR)
Explain the steps to manage a child who develops anaphylaxis after BCG. — Immediate epinephrine, airway, fluids, observe
Why is the inactivated influenza vaccine preferred over the live nasal spray in immunocompromised adults? — No risk of viral replication
Describe the rationale for using a conjugate Hib vaccine instead of plain polysaccharide in infants. — Induces T‑cell help, better immunogenicity
What is the protective antibody titre for measles? — ≥200 mIU/mL
How would you handle a suspected vaccine‑associated paralytic polio case? — Isolate, supportive care, report to national programme
Explain the impact of antigenic drift on influenza vaccine effectiveness. — Reduces match, necessitates annual reformulation
When is a booster dose of MMR recommended for a previously vaccinated child? — After 10 years or if exposure risk
What are the key components of a cold‑chain management plan in a rural clinic? — Temperature log, solar fridge, backup power, training
How do you interpret a low measles IgG titre in a child who received two doses? — Indicates non‑seroconversion; recommend booster
Why is the BCG vaccine given at birth in high TB prevalence areas? — Provides early protection against severe TB in children
